cases.notes: Roadmap and research outcomes with figures, and alignment claimed without one. Alignment is the competency most often asserted and least often measured, and the fixture keeps that asymmetry.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you decide what to build?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I rewrote our prioritisation model and cut the roadmap from 40 items to 12. What survived was the work we could actually staff.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Did that change how you work?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Every prioritisation call now takes 30 minutes. The arguments happen before the meeting rather than in it, which is where they used to happen.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about research.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: Our discovery research covered 18 customer interviews before we built anything. Half of them were with people who had already churned.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Did it change a decision?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: That research killed 2 features early. Nobody wrote a line of code for either of them, which saved a whole quarter of build time.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How do you keep stakeholders together?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I run stakeholder alignment sessions but I could not put a number on how well they work. People turn up, which is something.

evidence.quote_contains: I rewrote our prioritisation model and cut the roadmap from 40 items to 12
Every prioritisation call now takes 30 minutes
Our discovery research covered 18 customer interviews

cases.notes: One example under the floor, one admitted gap, one topic that never reached the candidate at all because it was handled above them.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about prioritisation you have owned.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I owned prioritisation for one 6 week experiment. It was a side bet rather than the main roadmap, and nobody senior was watching it closely.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: And customer research?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I do not know that I have a discovery research example that stands out. We mostly took the requirements as given.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How about stakeholders?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: That was handled above me. I saw the outcome rather than the conversation that produced it, and I was not in the room.

evidence.quote_contains: I owned prioritisation for one 6 week experiment
I do not know that I have a discovery research example

cases.notes: A genuine conflict about release count in one named year, with prioritisation evidence beside it.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How often did you ship?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: The team I supported shipped 14 releases that year. We were on a weekly train for most of it and the cadence almost never slipped.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Say that again for me.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: That year the team I supported shipped 6 releases. Each one was a big bundle rather than a small change.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: How did you choose what went in?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: My prioritisation framework ranks 5 dimensions. Reach and confidence are the two people argue about, and effort is the one nobody trusts.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Who else is in that conversation?

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: We reviewed the prioritisation list with 3 teams each month. Anything nobody would staff came off it, which made the list shorter and much more honest.

evidence.quote_contains: We reviewed the prioritisation list with 3 teams each month

contradictions.why: Fourteen releases and six releases, the same team and the same year.

cases.notes: A four word answer. There is nothing to measure and the right response is another question, not a low band.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Tell me about a prioritisation call you made.

turns.speaker: candidate
turns.text: I made a few.
